'''''Daphne laureola''''', commonly called '''spurge-laurel''',<ref name="PlantAtlas">{{cite web | title=Spurge-laurel ''Daphne laureola'' L. | website=PlantAtlas | url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.bte | access-date=2025-08-20}}</ref> is a woodland shrub in the [[flowering plant]] family [[Thymelaeaceae]]. Its native range covers much of western and southern Europe and extends to [[Algeria]], [[Morocco]] and the [[Azores]].<ref name="Euro+Med">{{cite web | last=Pedrol | first=J. | title=''Daphne laureola'' | website=Euro+Med-Plantbase | url=https://europlusmed.org/cdm_dataportal/taxon/a9e950cf-e9e9-4488-9264-1213e3cbd185 | access-date=2025-08-20}}</ref><ref name="POWO">{{cite web | title=''Daphne laureola'' L. | website=Plants of the World Online | url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:831270-1 | access-date=2025-08-20}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Daphne laureola, Spurge-laurel, Valbona Valley NP, Albania (31842280098).jpg|thumb|In fruit, [[Valbona Valley]], Albania]]
''Daphne laureola'' reaches a height between {{Convert|0.5-1|m|ft|0}}, rarely to 1.5 m. The habit of this shrub can be upright or [[decumbent]] (arched at the base then spreading upward). The bark is thin and yellow-grey when mature, while immature stems are green. The [[leaf|leaves]] are spirally arranged, usually forming dense whorls at the shoot tips, but may clothe the full length of the shoots. The leaves are [[oblanceolate]] to [[obovate]]-oblanceolate, {{Convert|5–12|cm|in|0}} long and 1–3 cm wide. They are [[glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]] (hairless), dark green and glossy on the upper surface, and lighter green beneath.<ref name="Blamey">{{cite book | last1=Blamey | first1=Marjorie | last2=Grey-Wilson | first2=Christopher | title=The Illustrated Flora of Britain and Northern Europe | publisher=Hodder & Stoughton | publication-place=London | date=1989 | isbn=0-340-40170-2 | page=244}}</ref><ref name="Streeter">{{cite book | last=Streeter | first=David | title=Flower Guide | publisher=Collins | publication-place=London | date=2010 | isbn=978-0-00-718389-0 | page=306}}</ref>

The flowers are 8–12 mm long, inconspicuous, yellow-green, with four sepals and no petals, and are honey-scented, produced in small axial racemes somewhat hidden among the leaf bases. Flowering is in late winter and early spring, with pollination by flies and moths; the plant is outcrossing, so seed production depends on multiple plants being present.<ref name="PlantAtlas" /><ref name="Blamey"/><ref name="Streeter"/> The berry is black, egg-shaped, and {{Convert|1.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} wide, containing one seed; it ripens in late summer, and is poisonous to humans, but not to birds, which eat the berries and disperse the seeds.<ref name="PlantAtlas" /><ref name="Blamey"/>

==Taxonomy==
Two [[subspecies]] are accepted by the [[Plants of the World Online]] database;<ref name="POWO"/> they are not considered distinct by the Euro+Med Plantbase, which treats the species as monotypic.<ref name="Euro+Med"/>
*''Daphne laureola'' subsp. ''laureola'' — most of the species' range
*''Daphne laureola'' subsp. ''philippi'' (Gren.) Nyman — restricted to the [[Pyrenees]]

== Etymology ==
The genus name ''Daphne'' is from the ancient [[Greek language|Greek]] for [[Laurus|laurel]]. [[Daphne]] is also the name of a [[dryad]] in [[Greek mythology]] who was transformed into a laurel tree. The specific epithet ''laureola'' means 'laurel-like'; therefore, the [[Binomial nomenclature|binomial]] translates to "laurel-like laurel".<ref name="gledhill">Gledhill, David (2008). "The Names of Plants". Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback).  pp 134, 232</ref> The English name spurge-laurel refers its superficial foliage resemblance to a laurel, and to its [[spurge]]-like [[purgative]] properties.<ref name="OED">{{cite book |author1-link=Oxford English Dictionary |title=Oxford English Dictionary |date=1884–1928 |publisher=Oxford University Press |page=S 712 |edition=1}}</ref>

== Ecology and habitat ==
It is one of two species of ''Daphne'' native to [[Great Britain]], the other being ''[[Daphne mezereum]]''. Both have a strong preference for [[alkaline soils]] and are most commonly found in [[limestone]] areas, although ''D. laureola'' is also found on clay.<ref name=Stac10>{{Cite book |last=Stace |first=Clive |authorlink = Clive Stace |year=2010 |title=New Flora of the British Isles |edition=3rd |location=Cambridge, UK |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-70772-5 }} pp. 381–382.</ref> However, unlike ''D. mezereum'', ''D. laureola'' is [[evergreen]], with yellowish-green flowers borne very early in the spring and black berries.<ref>The [[Reader's Digest]] Field Guide to the Trees and Shrubs of Britain ''p.123''.</ref>

==As an invasive species==
Outside its native range, ''D. laureola'' is [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in Scotland, Ireland,<ref name="PlantAtlas"/> Denmark, and Crimea.<ref name="Euro+Med"/> It has become an [[invasive weed]] in parts of Australasia and western North America. Growing in sun or shade, it is well-suited to the [[temperate]] [[forest]] [[understory]] and can colonise areas (both by seeding and by root [[Sucker (botany)|suckering]]) to form [[monotypic]] stands and out-compete native vegetation. It is a Class B [[Noxious weed]] in [[Washington state]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nwcb.wa.gov/weed_info/Daphne_laureola.html |title=Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board |accessdate=2008-09-09 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080821032600/http://www.nwcb.wa.gov/weed_info/Daphne_laureola.html |archivedate=2008-08-21 }}</ref> It is also a weed in native forests in Tasmania, Australia,<ref>{{Cite web|last=Baker|first=ML|date=January 2013|title=Daphne laureola L. (Thymelaeaceae): A weedy alien species new to Australia|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/290956450|via=ResearchGate}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=2021|title=Daphne Laurel|url=https://www.hobartcity.com.au/City-services/Environment/Environmental-weeds/Daphne-laurel|url-status=live|access-date=13 July 2021|website=Hobartcity.au|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210713031623/https://www.hobartcity.com.au/City-services/Environment/Environmental-weeds/Daphne-laurel |archive-date=2021-07-13 }}</ref> and New Zealand.<ref>{{cite web|date=2021|title=Green Daphne Laurel|url=https://www.weedbusters.org.nz/what-are-weeds/weed-list/green-daphne-laurel/|url-status=live|access-date=13 July 2021|website=Weed Busters New Zealand|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210202112738/https://www.weedbusters.org.nz/what-are-weeds/weed-list/green-daphne-laurel/ |archive-date=2021-02-02 }}</ref>

Hand-pulling is effective against small infestations (gloves must be worn to protect against the [[Corrosive substance|caustic]] sap); shrubs too large or too small to pull must be dug out.<ref name="ReferenceA">Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board: ''Daphne laureola''</ref>

==Toxicity==
All parts of the plant, including the fruit, are poisonous for humans. The [[sap]] is known to cause skin rashes on contact.<ref>{{cite web | title=''Daphne laureola'' Spurge Laurel PFAF Plant Database | website=pfaf.org | date=2007-08-30 | url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Daphne+laureola | access-date=2025-08-20}}</ref>

==In culture==
[[Gilbert White]] called it dwarf laurel, and on 5 December 1783 "fetched them" from the high wood and hanger at [[Selborne]] and planted them in his garden.<ref>The English Year, compiled by Geoffrey Grigson O.U.P 1967</ref>
